title: Job Openings and Labor Turnover, May 2026 (USDL-26-1123)
date_evidence: For release 10:00 a.m. (ET) Tuesday, June 30, 2026      USDL-26-1123
key_claim: US layoffs and discharges were unchanged at 1.7 million in May 2026, a rate of 1.1 percent, with job openings at 7.6 million, hires at 5.2 million and quits at 3.1 million.
frame_summary: The BLS release frames May 2026 as a labour market with historically low involuntary separations and little month-to-month movement, which is the measured baseline any claim about AI-driven displacement has to be reconciled against.
verbatim_quote: The number of layoffs and discharges was unchanged at 1.7 million, while the rate changed little at 1.1 percent in May.
verbatim_list: The number of job openings was unchanged at 7.6 million in May, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Hires were unchanged at 5.2 million, while total separations changed little at 5.1 million.
notes: Archived release URL is stable and carries a fixed reference month. Quotes captured from a live fetch on 2026-08-15; the Cowork sandbox shell has no network egress, so re-run the quote-provenance audit host-side.

title: Commission Staff Working Document SWD(2026) 239 final, accompanying the second-stage social partner consultation on quality jobs
date_evidence: EUROPEAN COMMISSION Brussels, 20.7.2026 SWD(2026) 239 final COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT
key_claim: The Commission has opened a second-stage consultation of EU social partners under Article 154(3) TFEU on possible EU action to improve job quality, with algorithmic management and AI at work identified as an area where workers' and business organisations are directly opposed on whether binding rules are needed.
frame_summary: The Commission frames workplace AI as a live legislative question rather than a settled one, which means an employer's own characterisation of an AI-driven workforce decision is being written into a rulemaking record while that record is still open.
verbatim_quote: This document accompanies the second stage consultation of the social partners at EU level, in accordance with Article 154(3) TFEU, to obtain their views on the possible content of EU action to improve the quality of jobs.
verbatim_list: On algorithmic management and artificial intelligence (AI) at work, there is a clear divide: workers’ organisations are pushing for more stringent and explicit rules to safeguard workers’ rights and wellbeing, while business organisations oppose additional binding rules, being concerned about regulatory burdens and prefer enhancing current frameworks through nonbinding instruments.
notes: PDF fetched live on 2026-08-15; quotes reproduced with PDF line breaks normalised to single spaces.

title: Challenger Report: Layoffs Fall, Hiring Picks Up; AI Leads For Fifth Straight Month
key_claim: US employers announced 33,429 job cuts in July 2026, the lowest monthly total in two years; AI led all stated reasons for the fifth consecutive month at 10,970 cuts or 33%, taking the year-to-date AI-attributed total to 112,713 of 477,033 announced cuts, and Challenger explicitly flagged the ambiguity of AI attribution in a disputed hospital case.
frame_summary: Challenger argues that AI has become the reason employers give rather than a measured cause, and that the label is chosen partly for its effect on investors, which makes the firm's own classification increasingly unreliable as regulation tightens.
verbatim_quote: In July, Artificial Intelligence (AI) led all reasons for job cuts, with 10,970 announced during the month, or 33%. It is the fifth consecutive month AI has been the leading reason. So far this year, AI has been cited in 112,713 job cut announcements, approximately 24% of all cuts.
verbatim_list: U.S.-based employers announced 33,429 job cuts in July, down 27% from the 45,849 cuts announced in June.
Through July, employers have announced 477,033 job cuts, down 41% from the 806,383 cuts announced in the first seven months of 2025.
The ambiguous nature of what constitutes AI-attributed cuts was highlighted in July.

Challenger uses this categorization when a company states new technology was the main reason for layoffs and AI is alluded to but not directly tied to the cuts. Challenger tracked 20,219 cuts for this reason in 2025.
Naming AI in a layoff announcement can win over investors while pushing current and prospective employees away. That’s why the messaging has swung from hedging to aggressively citing it,
As regulations start to take shape, companies will be even more careful in their announcements, which would make tracking the impact of AI on jobs more opaque,
Employers announced plans to hire 16,095 workers in July, up 47% from the 10,933 plans announced in June and well above the 3,200 announced in July 2025.
notes: Primary announcement-level data source for the scan, and the source that surfaces the classification problem in its own July file.

publisher: Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR)
title: What is really happening to jobs? Separating AI hype from reality
key_claim: SIEPR finds AI's effect on aggregate employment is likely small at present: unemployment among the most AI-exposed quintile rose 0.77 percentage points since 2022 against 0.85 points for the least exposed, only 5 percent of firms in Census data report any employment impact, and layoff announcements citing AI are met with scepticism by industry leaders and labour economists.
frame_summary: The brief argues that the measured labour market and the announced narrative have come apart, and that some AI-cited layoffs are better explained by cash-flow reallocation toward AI investment or by pandemic-era over-hiring than by automation itself.
verbatim_quote: While some narrow layoffs may be connected to AI-related automation, others appear driven by a desire to free up cash flow for AI investments or to reduce headcount after pandemic-era over-hiring.
verbatim_list: the unemployment rate for the top quintile of AI-exposed workers has risen by 0.77 percentage points since 2022, while the unemployment rate for the least-exposed workers rose slightly more, by 0.85 percentage points over the same period
In the Census data, only 5 percent of firms report any employment impact, with equal numbers reporting gains and losses.
Eighty percent of executives surveyed by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta said AI investments have yet to alter their headcount or improve productivity.
What about the companies announcing layoffs, increasingly citing AI as a driving factor? Both industry leaders and labor economists express some healthy skepticism about these claims.
notes: Fetched live on 2026-08-15. Page carries a Publication Date field of July, 2026; day-level precision is not published, so 1 July is recorded as the month start.

publisher: SSRN (Ding, Ma, Wu and Yang, University of Pittsburgh Katz Graduate School of Business)
title: Tracking Artificial Intelligence Sentiment in the U.S. Labor Market
date_evidence: 116 Pages Posted: 6 May 2026 Last revised: 11 Jun 2026
key_claim: Using Glassdoor reviews, earnings-call disclosures, LinkedIn profiles and job postings across 2021 to 2025, the authors find employee AI sentiment is significantly more negative than overall firm sentiment, that AI-related layoffs depress it further and can offset the benefits of adoption, and that firms with more AI-skilled employees show higher turnover and slower employment growth even excluding post-pandemic over-hirers.
frame_summary: The paper argues that the workforce effects of AI are real and traceable in firm-level data rather than being mainly a labelling artefact, and that employee sentiment is the channel through which an AI-attributed layoff destroys the productivity gain it was meant to secure.
verbatim_quote: These results are also true for firms without excessive hiring after the COVID pandemic, suggesting that the effects are not mainly due to AI washing.
verbatim_list: AI-related layoffs negatively affect employee AI sentiment and thus could offset the benefits of adopting AI.
Through a textual analysis of employee job reviews, we find that employee sentiment towards AI is significantly more negative than their overall sentiment towards firms.
notes: Structural anchor: posted 101 days before the scan date, just outside the soft 3-month window, and the canonical counter-evidence for the attribution argument. Cited inline like any other source.

title: A dozen Montefiore nurses in the Bronx are being pushed out by AI, union says
key_claim: Twelve Montefiore utilization review nurses received position-elimination notices dated 28 May; the New York State Nurses Association filed a class-action grievance on 1 June alleging breach of a contract clause requiring management to meet the union where AI diminishes union jobs, while Montefiore called the union's claims inaccurate and misleading and did not confirm that layoff notices were sent.
frame_summary: The report frames the dispute as one about attribution rather than about job losses: the contractual duty turns on whether AI caused the diminishment, and employer and union give opposite answers to that question.
verbatim_quote: The contract NYSNA reached with Montefiore following this year’s strike includes language stating that if the use of AI results in the “diminishment” of union jobs, hospital management must meet with the union to discuss a way to avoid that outcome.
verbatim_list: As is often the case, the claims by NYSNA are inaccurate and misleading,

NYSNA filed a class-action grievance with Montefiore on June 1, alleging that the hospital system violated its contract by failing to meet with the union before sending out notices about nurses’ jobs being eliminated.
notes: Fetched live on 2026-08-15. Same case Challenger classifies as Technological Update (possibly AI) in its July file.

title: AI Layoff Reversed? Should You Go Back To Your Old Job?
key_claim: Forbes reports that employers who cut roles on AI grounds are approaching former staff about returning, and advises workers to establish what has changed in the employer's AI position before accepting.
frame_summary: The piece treats the reversal of an AI-attributed cut as a normal enough occurrence to warrant standing career advice, which is itself evidence that the attribution is not holding.
notes: Used directionally only, for the existence and normalisation of AI-layoff reversals. No numerical claim is drawn from this source, so no verbatim_quote is recorded.
